title: Cyclic Vector Theorem: Factorization Bridge via Multiset UFD
description: Proves that the polynomial factorization bridge for the cyclic vector theorem can be proved without Finset as a primitive. Every monic polynomial of positive degree over a field factors into coprime monic irreducible prime powers — using UniqueFactorizationMonoid on K[X] and a recursive multiset-to-Finset conversion. Answers the open question from cayley-hamilton-cyclic-vector-all-fields: YES, the factorization bridge requires no deep Finset infrastructure.

meta.author: Lean Genius Research
meta.assumptions: No axioms or sorries. All proofs use Mathlib's UniqueFactorizationMonoid, Polynomial, and Matrix APIs.
originalContributions: monic_irreducible_multiset_factorization: factors any monic polynomial into a multiset of monic irreducibles via UniqueFactorizationMonoid.exists_prime_factors
finset_factorization_from_multiset: recursive induction converts a multiset of irreducibles into a Fin k-indexed family of distinct irreducibles with exponents
monic_factored_form: the complete factorization bridge — monic poly → coprime monic prime powers indexed by Fin k
nonderogatory_has_cyclic_vector: main theorem — over ANY field K, every nonderogatory matrix has a cyclic vector (uses primary decomposition from WIP04)
nonderogatory_has_cyclic_vector_finite: corollary — holds over finite fields F_q with q ≤ n where union avoidance fails
meta.historicalContext: A matrix M is nonderogatory if its minimal polynomial equals its characteristic polynomial. The cyclic vector theorem states that every nonderogatory matrix has a cyclic vector — a vector v such that {v, Mv, ..., M^(n-1)v} is a basis. Over infinite fields, the classical proof avoids finitely many hyperplanes. Over finite fields (where avoidance may fail), the proof requires a different approach. This formalization uses primary decomposition to give a single proof valid over all fields.
meta.proofStrategy: 1. Factor minpoly K M = ∏ p_i^{e_i} using monic_factored_form (via UFD on K[X] + recursive Finset-indexed grouping). 2. Apply WIP04's primary decomposition theorem (nonderogatory_general_has_cyclic_vector): for each primary component p_i^{e_i}, find a primary vector v_i in ker(p_i^{e_i}(M)) \ ker(p_i^{e_i-1}(M)). 3. CRT combination: v = Σ v_i is cyclic — any annihilator is divisible by each p_i^{e_i} via Bezout projections.

overview.problemStatement:
**Open question from cayley-hamilton-cyclic-vector-all-fields**: Can the polynomial factorization bridge — every monic polynomial of positive degree factors into coprime monic irreducible prime powers — be proved without Finset as a foundational primitive?

More precisely: can one prove
$$\mu = \prod_{i=1}^k p_i^{e_i}$$
where the $p_i$ are distinct monic irreducibles, the $e_i > 0$, and the factors are pairwise coprime, using only the UFD structure of $K[X]$ and multiset induction?
overview.historicalContext:
The cyclic vector theorem is a fundamental result in linear algebra: a matrix is *nonderogatory* (minimal polynomial equals characteristic polynomial) if and only if it has a cyclic vector $v$ — i.e., $\{v, Mv, M^2 v, \dots, M^{n-1} v\}$ spans $K^n$. The result was implicit in the classical work on canonical forms (Frobenius, *Über lineare Substitutionen und bilineare Formen*, *Crelle* 1878; Krull, *Zur Theorie der allgemeinen Zahlringe*, *Math. Annalen* 1928), and explicit in the rational canonical form theory of Hermann Weyl (*The Classical Groups*, 1939) and Felix Gantmacher (*The Theory of Matrices*, 1959). Over infinite fields, the textbook proof selects a vector $v = c_1 e_1 + \cdots + c_n e_n$ avoiding finitely many algebraic hyperplanes (one for each invariant subspace), which exists by a Vandermonde or generic-point argument. Over **finite fields with $|K| \le n$** — for instance, $\mathbb{F}_2$ for a $3 \times 3$ matrix — such avoidance can fail outright: a finite vector space is the union of its proper subspaces only in extreme cases, but those cases are exactly the ones a generic argument cannot rule out. The classical workaround was Jordan-decomposition-style: split into primary components and combine via the Chinese Remainder Theorem on $K[X]/\langle\mu\rangle$. This approach goes back at least to Curtis-Reiner *Representation Theory of Finite Groups and Associative Algebras* (1962, §4) and is the strategy formalized here.

The **technical bottleneck for formalization** is producing the factorization $\mu = \prod_i p_i^{e_i}$ (distinct monic irreducibles, positive exponents, pairwise coprime) in a form Lean's type system can consume — specifically, indexed by a `Fin k` so the primary decomposition lemma can quantify over the factors. The parent entry left this as an open question: can this be done without invoking deep `Finset` infrastructure? This file answers **yes**: `UniqueFactorizationMonoid` on $K[X]$ gives a `Multiset` of irreducibles, and a recursive multiset-to-`Fin k` induction (using decidable equality on $K[X]$) groups repeated factors into exponents. The rest of the proof — `nonderogatory_has_cyclic_vector` over any field — then becomes a straightforward application of the primary decomposition theorem from WIP04. The corollary for finite fields (`nonderogatory_has_cyclic_vector_finite`) is *free* in the sense that the proof never invokes $|K| > n$.
keyInsights: The UFD structure of $K[X]$ (via `UniqueFactorizationMonoid.exists_prime_factors`) gives a `Multiset` factorization. Converting this to a `Fin k`-indexed family with grouped exponents requires a careful induction on the multiset — a generic operation that the standard library doesn't provide directly.

The recursive induction in `finset_factorization_from_multiset` groups repeated irreducibles by incrementing their exponent, using decidable equality on $K[X]$ (a `by_cases` on `∃ i, p' i = p`). This is constructively explicit: each multiset element is examined in turn, and the running family is updated either by exponent increment (existing factor) or by appending (new factor).

The factorization bridge is proved entirely without explicitly invoking `Finset`'s API at the mathematical level — `Finset` only appears as the index type `Fin k` for the output family. This addresses the parent OQ's specific concern: deep `Finset` infrastructure is not needed.

The primary decomposition theorem (from WIP04) then takes the factored minpoly and constructs a cyclic vector, using **Bezout's identity in $K[X]$** to separate the primary components. The Bezout coefficients give projection maps onto each $\ker(p_i^{e_i}(M))$, and a sum of primary vectors $v = \sum v_i$ is cyclic because any annihilator is forced to be divisible by each $p_i^{e_i}$.

The finite field case is a *free* corollary: the proof never invokes $|K| > n$, working instead with the annihilator structure directly. Compare the classical infinite-field argument (avoiding hyperplanes), which fails for $\mathbb{F}_2$ on $3 \times 3$ matrices — the primary decomposition route is uniform across all field sizes.

**Structural lesson — multiset induction as a UFD-formalization primitive**: the multiset-to-`Fin k` recursion used here is reusable for *any* proof requiring a distinct-irreducible decomposition with grouped exponents (Jordan canonical form, primary decomposition of modules over a PID, $p$-adic valuations of integers). Extracting this as a Mathlib helper would shorten future formalizations of factorization-driven structure theorems.

**Why 'all fields' matters**: most Mathlib linear algebra results are stated over `Field K` without further assumptions, but many *proofs* implicitly assume infinity (via `Fintype` avoidance arguments). This entry produces an explicit witness that the cyclic vector theorem belongs to the class of results that hold uniformly — a useful data point for Mathlib's general program of removing infinity hypotheses where possible.
overview.proofStrategy:
Step 1 (monic_irreducible_multiset_factorization): Use UniqueFactorizationMonoid.exists_prime_factors to factor μ into a multiset of irreducibles. Normalize to monic by multiplying by C(leadingCoeff)⁻¹.

Step 2 (finset_factorization_from_multiset): Induct on the multiset. Base: empty — contradiction (f ≠ 0). Singleton: k=1, p=[p], e=[1]. Inductive: if the new irreducible matches p_i in the existing family, increment e_i; otherwise append it with exponent 1.

Step 3 (monic_factored_form): Compose steps 1 and 2. Add coprimality via coprime_pow_of_coprime_irreducible.

Step 4 (nonderogatory_has_cyclic_vector): Factor minpoly K M, then apply the primary decomposition theorem from WIP04.
prerequisites: UniqueFactorizationMonoid.exists_prime_factors: K[X] is a UFD, so any nonzero polynomial factors into irreducibles
IsCoprime.pow: coprimality is preserved under powers
Matrix.isIntegral: matrices are integral elements (minpoly is well-defined)
openQuestions: **Splitting field shortcut**: Can the factorization bridge be further simplified using `Polynomial.roots` (Mathlib) and splitting fields to avoid the multiset induction entirely? Concretely, in the splitting field $L \supseteq K$ of $\mu$, the polynomial factors completely into linear factors; Galois-descent could in principle recover a $K$-irreducible factorization. The trade-off: splitting fields are heavy machinery, so the gain in code length is uncertain.

**Generalize to PIDs**: Does the primary decomposition approach extend to modules over arbitrary commutative Noetherian rings (not just fields)? The result would be a module-theoretic cyclic vector theorem — for a finitely generated torsion module $M$ over a PID, the existence of an element $m \in M$ generating $M$ as a module over $R[X]$ when $M$ is *cyclic-as-defined* by its torsion structure. This connects to Smith normal form and the structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a PID.

**Mathlib's rational canonical form**: Is there a Mathlib formalization of the rational canonical form (RCF) that could simplify this proof further? The RCF directly gives a cyclic-vector decomposition for any matrix, and the nonderogatory case is a single-block special case. As of 2026, Mathlib has Smith normal form and the structure theorem for modules over PIDs but not the RCF specifically; integrating the two would be a useful Mathlib contribution.

**Reusable multiset-to-`Fin k` lemma**: Can the multiset-to-`Fin k` induction (`finset_factorization_from_multiset`) be extracted as a generic Mathlib lemma usable for *any* UFD factorization with grouped exponents? Generic statement: given `M : Multiset α` and `[DecidableEq α]`, produce `(k : ℕ) (f : Fin k → α) (e : Fin k → ℕ)` with `f` injective, `e i > 0`, and `M = ∑ i, e i • {f i}`.

**Non-nonderogatory generalization**: Can the cyclic vector theorem be extended to the non-nonderogatory case — existence of a *generating set* of cyclic vectors matching the invariant factor structure? For a general matrix $M$ with invariant factors $f_1 \mid f_2 \mid \cdots \mid f_r$, the conjecture is that there exist vectors $v_1, \dots, v_r$ such that the union $\bigcup_i \{v_i, M v_i, \dots, M^{\deg f_i - 1} v_i\}$ is a basis.

sections.title: Definitions
sections.summary: IsCyclicVector: v is cyclic for M if no nonzero polynomial of degree < n annihilates both. IsNonderogatory: minpoly = charpoly.
sections.mathContext: A vector v ∈ Kⁿ is cyclic for M if {v, Mv, ..., M^(n-1)v} spans Kⁿ. Equivalently, the only polynomial of degree < n annihilating v is the zero polynomial. These are delegated to GeneralCyclicVector's definitions from WIP04.

sections.title: Polynomial Factorization Bridge
sections.summary: Proves monic_factored_form: every monic polynomial of positive degree factors into coprime monic irreducible prime powers. Key lemmas: monic_irreducible_multiset_factorization (UFD multiset factor), finset_factorization_from_multiset (recursive Fin-indexed grouping), coprime_of_distinct_monic_irreducible, coprime_pow_of_coprime_irreducible.
sections.mathContext: The factorization exists because K[X] is a UFD. The challenge is converting the abstract multiset of irreducibles into a Fin k-indexed family with distinct elements and grouped exponents — this uses decidable equality on K[X] and induction on the multiset.

sections.title: Main Theorem and Corollaries
sections.summary: nonderogatory_has_cyclic_vector: main theorem over ANY field (including finite). nonderogatory_has_cyclic_vector_finite: corollary for finite fields. cyclic_iff_not_killed_below_degree: characterization via degree bound.
sections.mathContext: The main proof: factor minpoly K M via monic_factored_form, then apply WIP04's primary decomposition to get the cyclic vector. The finite field corollary is immediate since the proof never invokes |K| > n. The characterization corollary unwraps the definition of IsCyclicVector.

crossReferences.description: Imports the primary decomposition theorem (nonderogatory_general_has_cyclic_vector) from WIP04. That file proves the cyclic vector exists given a factored minpoly via Bezout projections. This entry provides the factorization bridge that WIP04 depends on.

Foundational: every matrix M satisfies its characteristic polynomial χ_M(M) = 0. The nonderogatory condition (minpoly = charpoly) implies every v is 'almost cyclic' — the Cayley-Hamilton theorem bounds the degree of annihilating polynomials.
Parent open question: this entry answers the factorization bridge sub-question and provides the complete axiom-free proof of the cyclic vector theorem over all fields.

conclusion.summary: The factorization bridge is fully proved without deep Finset infrastructure. The proof uses UniqueFactorizationMonoid on K[X] and a recursive multiset-to-Fin induction. The main theorem nonderogatory_has_cyclic_vector holds over any field — including finite fields where |K| ≤ n — because the primary decomposition approach bypasses the union-avoidance argument used in classical infinite-field proofs.
conclusion.implications: This completes the cyclic vector theorem in Lean with 0 sorries and 0 axioms. The approach demonstrates that polynomial factorization over a UFD can be formalized at a relatively low cost (~50 lines for the bridge) using multiset induction and decidable equality. The technique is reusable for other proofs requiring distinct-irreducible decompositions.
openQuestions: Can the cyclic vector theorem be extended to the non-nonderogatory case (existence of a generating set of cyclic vectors matching the invariant factor structure)?
Is there a Mathlib formalization of the rational canonical form that could simplify this proof further?
